newsitem.title: USA: U.S. economic risks tilted to the upside - Broaddus.
newsitem.headline: U.S. economic risks tilted to the upside - Broaddus.

text.p: The U.S. economy is robust with tight labor markets across the board but still not showing any significant bottlenecks, said Alfred Broaddus, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond.
The risks, however, are tilted to the upside.
A summary of two speechs and briefings with journalists given by the Richmond Fed president this week shows he remains concerned about the pace of growth of the U.S. economy.
"My own feeling is that currently most of the risk in the outlook (for the economy in 1997) is on the upside ... with the possibility of rising inflationary pressures," he said.
"The economy is already operating in a high level. There is not much headroom for further acceleration in growth," Broaddus added.

Citing a consensus of professional forecasters and emphasizing that most of the economic momentum seen in the last quarter of 1996 has kept up through the first quarter of 1997, Broaddus drew a rosy outlook for the U.S. economy this year.
The Fed official said Gross Domestic Product (GDP) is expected to grow by a little less than three percent, slightly slower than the little-over-3.0-percent rate seen in 1996.

Broaddus said if such growth rate materialized, labor markets were expected to remain very tight, with the unemployment rate dropping to the vicinity of 5.0 percent, against the current 5.2 percent rate.
The Richmond Fed chief also said the housing sector is expected to have a "reasonably good year" in 1997. He said, however, that inflation is not expected to boom.
Broaddus said consumer inflation is expected to have a marginal uptick in 1997, with the core rate for the consumer price index (CPI) projected to remain below three percent.
The core CPI measures consumer inflation but excludes energy and food prices, which are considered a volatile series of economic indicators.
"It's a very optimistic forecast and there is no technical reason why we couldn't get an outcome like this in the year ahead and I certainly hope we do," Broaddus said.
Although inflation is expected to remain relatively under control in 1997, Broaddus said that most of the factors holding prices and wages down may be "temporary rather than permanent."

Among the factors keeping wage costs down, Broaddus cited job insecurity, which has prevented many American workers from demanding higher wages "as they would have in this kind of condition in some earlier business cycles."
Broaddus also said the development of Health Maintenance Organization (HMOs) has helped to keep down the growth of the main non-wage portion of labor costs.
Although he would not comment on the future course of monetary policy, Broaddus stressed at the end of his two speeches this week that the Fed must be ahead of the inflation curve.

"The time to fight inflation is precisely when there isn't much inflation ... It's important to the nation's economic welfare that we stay ahead of the inflation curve in conducting monetary policy," Broaddus said.

Broaddus is a member of the Federal Reserve's policy setting body, the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC). According to the rotation rules of the committee, Broaddus is scheduled to vote on policy actions in 1997.
The Fed raised the key federal funds rate by 25 basis points to 5.50 percent at the last FOMC meeting on March 25. The committee is scheduled to meet again on May 20.
